subject: chemistry

items.q: What holds the hydrogen atom and the chlorine atom together in a molecule of hydrogen chloride, HCl?
items.correct: The electrostatic attraction of both nuclei to a shared pair of electrons
items.misconception: The need of each atom to gain a full outer shell by sharing a pair of electrons
items.why: School chemistry often introduces bonding through the octet rule and uses anthropomorphic language ('atoms want to be stable', 'the atom needs one more electron'). This framework is widely reported in chemistry-education research as the dominant way students explain bonding, and it replaces an explanation in terms of electrostatic forces. Explain bonding by forces. The shared pair lies between the two nuclei and is attracted to both, so the nuclei are held together. The octet rule only summarizes a common result, and it has exceptions (BF₃, BeCl₂).
items.specStatementText: A covalent bond is formed by the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positively charged nuclei. The octet rule refers to the tendency of atoms to gain a valence shell with a total of 8 electrons.
items.random_wrong: The shared pair of electrons itself, acting as a physical link between the atoms

items.q: Boron trichloride, BCl₃, is a covalent molecule (boron is in group 13; chlorine is in group 17). In its Lewis formula, how many electrons are in the valence shell of the boron atom?
items.correct: 6 electrons, as boron forms three bonding pairs and has no lone pair
items.misconception: 8 electrons, as one B–Cl bond must be a double bond to give boron an octet
items.why:
The octet rule is taught early and used repeatedly as a checking tool, so students treat it as an absolute requirement rather than a common pattern. Use the octet rule as a guide. An atom's valence electrons limit how many bonds it can form: boron has only three, so in BF₃ it forms three bonds and has six electrons, an incomplete octet.

Working: Boron has 3 valence electrons and forms one single bond to each Cl atom: 3 bonding pairs × 2 = 6 electrons, with no lone pair left. (Check: total valence electrons 3 + 3 × 7 = 24 = 3 bonding pairs (6) + 9 lone pairs on Cl (18).) Boron has 6 electrons, an incomplete octet.
items.specStatementText: A covalent bond is formed by the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positively charged nuclei. The octet rule refers to the tendency of atoms to gain a valence shell with a total of 8 electrons.
items.random_wrong: 3 electrons, as boron has three valence electrons of its own
items.working: Boron has 3 valence electrons and forms one single bond to each Cl atom: 3 bonding pairs × 2 = 6 electrons, with no lone pair left. (Check: total valence electrons 3 + 3 × 7 = 24 = 3 bonding pairs (6) + 9 lone pairs on Cl (18).) Boron has 6 electrons, an incomplete octet.

items.q: How does the carbon–carbon bond in ethyne, HC≡CH, compare with the carbon–carbon bond in ethane, CH₃CH₃?
items.correct: It is shorter and stronger
items.misconception: It is longer and stronger
items.why: Everyday reasoning suggests that putting more of something between two objects pushes them further apart, and in drawings a double bond looks 'bigger' than a single bond. More shared electron pairs means more negative charge between the two nuclei, so a greater attraction pulling the nuclei together: the bond is shorter as well as stronger.
items.specStatementText: Single, double and triple bonds involve one, two and three shared pairs of electrons respectively.
items.random_wrong: It is shorter and weaker

items.q: In the vapour at lower temperatures, aluminium chloride exists as Al₂Cl₆ molecules, formed when two AlCl₃ units join through two bridging chlorine atoms. Which describes the new bonds that join the two units?
items.correct: A lone pair on a chlorine atom of each unit is donated to the aluminium atom of the other
items.misconception: A lone pair on the aluminium atom of each unit is donated to a chlorine atom of the other unit
items.why: In ionic bonding metals lose electrons, so students carry over the idea that the metal is always the electron-giver. Look for the lone pair. Only an atom with a lone pair can donate one. In AlCl₃ the aluminium atom has six valence electrons and no lone pair, so it accepts; chlorine donates.
items.specStatementText: A coordination bond is a covalent bond in which both the electrons of the shared pair originate from the same atom.
items.random_wrong: Al³⁺ ions in one unit attract Cl⁻ ions in the other unit, forming two ionic bonds

items.q: Ammonia, NH₃, has three bonding pairs and one lone pair around the nitrogen atom. What is its molecular geometry?
items.correct: Trigonal pyramidal, as the lone pair occupies one of four tetrahedral domains
items.misconception: Tetrahedral, as there are four electron domains around the nitrogen atom
items.why: Students correctly learn that lone pairs count when arranging electron domains and then use that arrangement as the name of the shape, not realizing that the shape is named from the atoms. Two steps: arrange all domains (electron-domain geometry), then describe where the atoms are (molecular geometry). Lone pairs influence the shape but are not part of its name.
items.specStatementText: The valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) model enables the shapes of molecules to be predicted from the repulsion of electron domains around a central atom.
items.random_wrong: Trigonal planar, as only the three bonding pairs repel one another

items.q: Predict the H–O–H bond angle in a water molecule, H₂O.
items.correct: About 104.5°, as lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs do
items.misconception: About 109.5°, as all four electron domains around O repel one another equally
items.why: The ideal angles are learned first and are the only ones used in most diagrams, so students assume they apply whatever the domains contain. Rank the repulsions: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bonding pair > bonding pair–bonding pair, and a multiple bond repels more than a single bond. Stronger repulsion squeezes the other angles below the ideal values.
items.specStatementText: The valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) model enables the shapes of molecules to be predicted from the repulsion of electron domains around a central atom.
items.random_wrong: About 180°, as the two bonding pairs get as far apart as possible

items.q: In methanal, H₂CO, the carbon atom forms a single bond to each of two hydrogen atoms and a double bond to the oxygen atom. What is the best prediction of the H–C–H bond angle?
items.correct: Slightly less than 120°, as the C=O double bond repels more than a single bond
items.misconception: About 109.5°, as the two bonds of C=O count as two separate electron domains
items.why: Students count bond lines in the Lewis formula, and carbon's four bonds suggest 'four domains' by analogy with CH₄. Count the regions of electron density, not the lines: each atom attached to the central atom counts as one domain however many shared pairs join them, and each lone pair counts as one domain.
items.specStatementText: The valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) model enables the shapes of molecules to be predicted from the repulsion of electron domains around a central atom.
items.random_wrong: Exactly 120°, as all three electron domains around carbon repel equally

items.q: Electronegativity values: H 2.2, C 2.6, O 3.4, F 4.0, P 2.2. Which bond is the most polar?
items.correct: C–F
items.misconception: O–H
items.why: Hydrogen bonding is taught as arising from 'very polar' bonds between H and N, O or F, so students rank these bonds above all others without comparing the values. Compare electronegativity differences directly. Hydrogen bonding needs an H atom on N, O or F, but other bonds (such as C–F) can be more polar.
items.specStatementText: Bond polarity results from the difference in electronegativities of the bonded atoms.
items.random_wrong: O–F

items.q: Carbon dioxide, CO₂, has no net dipole moment (electronegativity: C 2.6, O 3.4). Which statement explains this?
items.correct: Its two C=O bond dipoles are equal and point in opposite directions, so they cancel
items.misconception: Its C=O bonds are non-polar, as the electronegativity difference is below 1.8
items.why: A rough numerical boundary between ionic and covalent bonding is often quoted, and students read 'covalent' as meaning 'equal sharing'. Separate the two ideas. Covalent bonds can be polar. The C=O bond (difference 0.8) is clearly polar, with δ− on oxygen.
items.specStatementText: Molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity and molecular geometry.
items.random_wrong: It carries no overall charge, so no separation of charge can exist in the molecule

items.q: Water, H₂O, has a net dipole moment (electronegativity: H 2.2, O 3.4). Which statement explains this?
items.correct: It is bent, so its two O–H bond dipoles do not point in opposite directions
items.misconception: Its O–H bonds are polar, and every molecule with polar bonds has a net dipole
items.why: Bond polarity is taught first, and the word 'polar' is applied to both bonds and molecules, so students transfer the property of the bonds directly to the molecule. Treat bond dipoles as vectors and add them using the molecular geometry. Only if they do not cancel does the molecule have a net dipole.
items.specStatementText: Molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity and molecular geometry.
items.random_wrong: Its H atoms lie at 90° to each other, as in its Lewis formula, so the dipoles add

items.q: Graphite conducts electricity. Which feature of its structure explains this?
items.correct: Each carbon atom bonds to three others, leaving one electron per atom delocalized
items.misconception: It contains carbon ions that move through the layers when a voltage is applied
items.why: The only non-metal conduction students have studied is conduction by ions in electrolytes, and graphite is used as electrodes in electrolysis, which links it with ions. Conduction needs mobile charged particles: ions in electrolytes, delocalized electrons in metals and in graphite. Graphite conducts by delocalized electrons, and no ions are present.
items.specStatementText: Carbon and silicon form covalent network structures.
items.random_wrong: Its atoms are held by metallic bonding, as its shiny grey appearance suggests

items.q: Which statement about carbon allotropes or silicon is correct?
items.correct: Graphene conducts electricity as each atom bonds to three others, leaving delocalized electrons
items.misconception: Diamond has a very high melting point because of strong intermolecular forces
items.why: Students learn that melting simple molecular substances overcomes intermolecular forces and generalize this to all covalent substances. First decide the structure. In a covalent network every atom is joined to its neighbours by covalent bonds, so melting breaks covalent bonds, which needs a great deal of energy.
items.specStatementText: Carbon and silicon form covalent network structures.
items.random_wrong: C₆₀ fullerene is a giant covalent network, so like diamond it dissolves in no solvent

items.q: Carbon dioxide sublimes at −78 °C, but silicon dioxide melts at about 1700 °C. Which statement explains the difference?
items.correct: SiO₂ is a giant covalent network, but CO₂ is made of small separate molecules
items.misconception: Subliming CO₂ breaks its C=O bonds, which are weaker than the Si–O bonds in SiO₂
items.why: Students hear that 'bonds are broken' when a substance changes state and do not separate bonds within molecules from forces between them. This is one of the most widely reported misconceptions in chemistry-education research on bonding. Distinguish intramolecular bonds from intermolecular forces. Boiling separates molecules from each other; the composition of the vapour is the same as that of the liquid.
items.specStatementText: Carbon and silicon form covalent network structures.
items.random_wrong: SiO₂ molecules are heavier than CO₂ molecules, so their London forces are stronger

items.q: Hydrogen chloride gas is mixed with iodine vapour. Which intermolecular forces act between an HCl molecule and an I₂ molecule?
items.correct: London and dipole–induced dipole forces, as HCl polarizes the I₂ molecule
items.misconception: London forces only, as I₂ is a non-polar molecule with no dipole
items.why: Students assign the force type to each substance separately (I₂ is 'London only') rather than to each pair of interacting molecules. Decide the force for each pair. HCl (permanent dipole) next to I₂ (polarizable) gives dipole–induced dipole forces, plus London forces.
items.specStatementText: The nature of the force that exists between molecules is determined by the size and polarity of the molecules. Intermolecular forces include London (dispersion), dipole-induced dipole, dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding.
items.random_wrong: London and dipole–dipole forces, as the HCl molecules are polar

items.q: Liquid methanol, CH₃OH, contains hydrogen bonds. What is a hydrogen bond in methanol?
items.correct: An attraction between the H of an O–H group and a lone pair on O in another molecule
items.misconception: The covalent bond between the O atom and the H atom within one methanol molecule
items.why: The name 'hydrogen bond' sounds like any bond involving hydrogen, and textbooks draw the O–H covalent bond and the hydrogen bond side by side. Locate the hydrogen bond between molecules: it links the H of one molecule to an O, N or F of another, and is much weaker than the covalent O–H bond.
items.specStatementText: The nature of the force that exists between molecules is determined by the size and polarity of the molecules. Intermolecular forces include London (dispersion), dipole-induced dipole, dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding.
items.random_wrong: An attraction between the H atoms of one molecule and the H atoms of another

items.q: Which statement about the intermolecular forces between molecules of propanone, CH₃COCH₃, is correct?
items.correct: They include dipole–dipole forces, which count as van der Waals forces
items.misconception: They include hydrogen bonds, as each propanone molecule contains H and O atoms
items.why: The rule is often remembered as a list of elements ('H with N, O or F') without the condition that the H must be bonded to one of them. Look at what each H atom is bonded to. Only H–N, H–O or H–F hydrogens are δ+ enough to form hydrogen bonds.
items.specStatementText: The nature of the force that exists between molecules is determined by the size and polarity of the molecules. Intermolecular forces include London (dispersion), dipole-induced dipole, dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding.
items.random_wrong: They include no London forces, as propanone molecules are polar

items.q: Propane, CH₃CH₂CH₃ (M_r 44.11), ethanal, CH₃CHO (M_r 44.06), and ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH (M_r 46.08), have comparable molar masses. Which lists them in order of increasing boiling point?
items.correct: propane < ethanal < ethanol
items.misconception: ethanal < propane < ethanol
items.why: The trend in boiling point with molar mass within a homologous series or down a group is taught first and is the easiest rule to apply. When molar masses are comparable, compare the strongest intermolecular force each substance has.
items.specStatementText: Given comparable molar mass, the relative strengths of intermolecular forces are generally: London (dispersion) forces < dipole–dipole forces < hydrogen bonding.
items.random_wrong: propane < ethanol < ethanal

items.q: Which of the following conducts electricity?
items.correct: Solid graphite
items.misconception: Liquid sulfur
items.why: The electrolysis of molten ionic compounds is a memorable demonstration, and students generalize 'molten substances conduct' to all substances. Ask what the mobile particles would be. Melting sulfur gives mobile S₈ molecules, which are neutral, so no current flows.
items.specStatementText: Given comparable molar mass, the relative strengths of intermolecular forces are generally: London (dispersion) forces < dipole–dipole forces < hydrogen bonding.
items.random_wrong: Diamond crystal

items.q: Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, mixes with water in all proportions, but hexane, C₆H₁₄, does not dissolve in water. Which statement explains this difference?
items.correct: Ethanol can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, but hexane cannot
items.misconception: Ethanol splits into ions that water surrounds, but hexane does not form ions
items.why: Dissolving is first met with salts, where the ions separate, and 'dissociation' and 'dissolving' are used almost interchangeably. Distinguish dissolving from ionizing. Most soluble covalent substances (ethanol, glucose) dissolve as molecules held among water molecules by hydrogen bonds.
items.specStatementText: Given comparable molar mass, the relative strengths of intermolecular forces are generally: London (dispersion) forces < dipole–dipole forces < hydrogen bonding.
items.random_wrong: Hexane is less dense than water, so it floats on the water rather than dissolving

items.q: In a paper chromatography experiment the baseline was drawn 1.0 cm above the bottom edge of the paper. At the end, the solvent front was 11.0 cm above the bottom edge and the centre of a spot was 4.4 cm above the bottom edge. What is the RF value of the spot?
items.why:
Students remember that RF is a ratio of the two distances but not which way up, and they do not check that the answer lies between 0 and 1. Put the component on top: RF = component distance ÷ solvent distance. An RF greater than 1 is impossible.

Working: Distance moved by spot = 4.4 cm − 1.0 cm = 3.4 cm. Distance moved by solvent = 11.0 cm − 1.0 cm = 10.0 cm. RF = 3.4 cm ÷ 10.0 cm = 0.34 (no units).
items.specStatementText: Chromatography is a technique used to separate the components of a mixture based on their relative attractions involving intermolecular forces to mobile and stationary phases.
items.working: Distance moved by spot = 4.4 cm − 1.0 cm = 3.4 cm. Distance moved by solvent = 11.0 cm − 1.0 cm = 10.0 cm. RF = 3.4 cm ÷ 10.0 cm = 0.34 (no units).

items.q: A mixture is separated by paper chromatography. Under the same conditions, component X has an RF value of 0.20 and component Y has an RF value of 0.75. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Relative to the mobile phase, X is attracted more strongly to the stationary phase than Y is
items.misconception: X has larger molecules than Y, so the fibres of the paper hold X back more than Y
items.why: The paper resembles a filter, and filtering separates by particle size, so students transfer that mechanism. Explain RF values by attractions: a component with a stronger attraction to the stationary phase (relative to the mobile phase) moves more slowly.
items.specStatementText: Chromatography is a technique used to separate the components of a mixture based on their relative attractions involving intermolecular forces to mobile and stationary phases.
items.random_wrong: X would also reach an RF of 0.75 if the solvent were allowed to run for a longer time

items.q: Ozone, O₃, can be represented by two Lewis formulas that differ only in which O–O bond is shown as the double bond. Which describes the bonds in a real ozone molecule?
items.correct: Two identical bonds, intermediate between single and double, as electrons are delocalized
items.misconception: One single and one double bond, fixed in place exactly as one of the two Lewis formulas shows
items.why: A single Lewis formula is usually drawn to represent the species, and students take that drawing literally. Use the measured bond lengths: identical bonds, intermediate between single and double, show that the electrons are delocalized.
items.specStatementText: Resonance structures occur when there is more than one possible position for a double bond in a molecule.
items.random_wrong: Two double bonds, with the central oxygen atom expanding its octet to ten electrons

items.q: In the ethanoate ion, CH₃COO⁻, the carbon atom of the COO group is bonded to the CH₃ carbon and to both O atoms. How many resonance structures can be deduced for the ethanoate ion?
items.correct: 2 structures, as the C=O double bond can be drawn to either O atom
items.misconception: 0 structures, as the atoms bonded to the central C are not all the same
items.why:
The standard examples of resonance (O₃, NO₃⁻, CO₃²⁻) are all symmetrical, with identical atoms around one central atom, and students take this symmetry, rather than the choice of positions for the double bond, as the condition for resonance. Look for a double bond that could be drawn to two or more equivalent atoms without moving any atom; the rest of the species need not be symmetrical.

Working: Valence electrons: 2 × C 4 + 3 × H 1 + 2 × O 6 + 1 (charge) = 24. The Lewis formula has three C–H bonds, a C–C bond, one C=O double bond and one C–O single bond, the singly bonded O carrying the −1 formal charge. The two O atoms are equivalent, so the double bond can be drawn to either of them: 2 resonance structures. A double bond to both O atoms would give carbon ten electrons (not possible in period 2), and moving an H atom changes the positions of atoms, giving a different species.
items.specStatementText: Resonance structures occur when there is more than one possible position for a double bond in a molecule.
items.random_wrong: 3 structures, as C can also form double bonds to both O atoms at once
items.working: Valence electrons: 2 × C 4 + 3 × H 1 + 2 × O 6 + 1 (charge) = 24. The Lewis formula has three C–H bonds, a C–C bond, one C=O double bond and one C–O single bond, the singly bonded O carrying the −1 formal charge. The two O atoms are equivalent, so the double bond can be drawn to either of them: 2 resonance structures. A double bond to both O atoms would give carbon ten electrons (not possible in period 2), and moving an H atom changes the positions of atoms, giving a different species.

items.q: The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of cyclohexene (one C=C bond) is about −120 kJ mol⁻¹. For benzene, forming cyclohexane, it is about −208 kJ mol⁻¹, much less exothermic than the −360 kJ mol⁻¹ predicted for a structure with three localized C=C bonds. Which statement explains the difference?
items.correct: Delocalization lowers benzene's energy, so less energy is released as it is hydrogenated
items.misconception: Breaking benzene's delocalized bonds releases less energy than breaking three C=C bonds
items.why: Everyday language speaks of energy 'stored in bonds' (for example in food or fuels) that is 'released' when the bonds break. This misconception is widely reported in chemistry-education research. Energy is absorbed to break bonds and released when bonds form. Benzene releases less energy on hydrogenation because it starts at a lower energy (it is stabilized by delocalization).
items.specStatementText: Benzene, C₆H₆, is an important example of a molecule that has resonance.
items.random_wrong: Benzene has only one or two C=C bonds, since 208 lies between 1 × 120 and 2 × 120

items.q: Cyclohexene reacts with bromine by addition. Benzene reacts with bromine only in the presence of a catalyst, and then by substitution, forming C₆H₅Br and HBr. Which statement explains why benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition?
items.correct: Substitution leaves benzene's delocalized ring of π electrons, and its stability, intact
items.misconception: Benzene has no π electrons at all, so like an alkane it can only take part in substitution
items.why: Students are told that benzene 'does not have alternating double bonds' and conclude that it has no π electrons at all. Benzene has π electrons, delocalized around the ring. This is why it reacts, but by substitution, which keeps the delocalized system.
items.specStatementText: Benzene, C₆H₆, is an important example of a molecule that has resonance.
items.random_wrong: Benzene contains three C=C bonds that are far stronger than the C=C bond in cyclohexene itself

items.q: In sulfur tetrafluoride, SF₄, the sulfur atom (six valence electrons) forms a single bond to each of four fluorine atoms. What is the molecular geometry of SF₄?
items.correct: See-saw, as the lone pair takes an equatorial site in a trigonal bipyramid
items.misconception: Tetrahedral, as only the four bonding pairs repel one another around sulfur
items.why: Lone pairs are often omitted from structural formulas and are invisible in ball-and-stick models, so students count only the atoms attached to the central atom. Count every electron domain around the central atom, including lone pairs, before predicting the shape.
items.specStatementText: Some atoms can form molecules in which they have an expanded octet of electrons.
items.random_wrong: Trigonal bipyramidal, as there are five electron domains around the sulfur atom

items.q: In xenon tetrafluoride, XeF₄, the xenon atom (eight valence electrons) forms a single bond to each of four fluorine atoms. What is the molecular geometry of XeF₄?
items.correct: Square planar, as the two lone pairs occupy opposite positions of an octahedron
items.misconception: See-saw, as the two lone pairs occupy adjacent positions, 90° apart, in an octahedron
items.why: All six positions of an octahedron are equivalent for the first lone pair, so students assume the second lone pair is also free to go anywhere. Place lone pairs to be as far apart as possible: in an octahedron that means opposite each other.
items.specStatementText: Some atoms can form molecules in which they have an expanded octet of electrons.
items.random_wrong: Tetrahedral, as only its four bonding pairs repel one another around the Xe atom

items.q: In the Lewis formula of carbon monoxide, C and O are joined by a triple bond and each atom has one lone pair. Using FC = V − N − ½B (V = valence electrons of the free atom, N = non-bonding electrons, B = bonding electrons), what is the formal charge on the carbon atom?
items.why:
Students think of charge as 'electrons gained', so they subtract in the order that counts extra electrons as positive. Start from the valence electrons of the free atom and subtract the electrons assigned to it: FC = V − N − ½B. Having more electrons than V gives a negative formal charge.

Working: Carbon: V = 4; N = 2 (one lone pair); B = 6 (triple bond). FC = V − N − ½B = 4 − 2 − 3 = −1. (Oxygen: 6 − 2 − 3 = +1; the sum, 0, equals the charge of the molecule.)
items.specStatementText: Formal charge values can be calculated for each atom in a species and used to determine which of several possible Lewis formulas is preferred.
items.working: Carbon: V = 4; N = 2 (one lone pair); B = 6 (triple bond). FC = V − N − ½B = 4 − 2 − 3 = −1. (Oxygen: 6 − 2 − 3 = +1; the sum, 0, equals the charge of the molecule.)

items.q: Two Lewis formulas are proposed for CO₂. In formula I, each O atom is joined to C by a double bond and has two lone pairs. In formula II, one O atom is joined to C by a triple bond and has one lone pair, and the other O atom is joined by a single bond and has three lone pairs. Which formula is preferred, and why?
items.correct: Formula I, as every atom in it has a formal charge of zero
items.misconception: Formula I, as the sum of all its formal charges is zero
items.why: Students are taught to check that the formal charges add up to the overall charge, and this check is the formal-charge rule they apply most often, so they mistake it for the rule for choosing between formulas. First make sure the sum equals the overall charge, then choose the formula whose individual formal charges are closest to zero.
items.specStatementText: Formal charge values can be calculated for each atom in a species and used to determine which of several possible Lewis formulas is preferred.
items.random_wrong: Formula II, as it places a negative formal charge on an oxygen atom

items.q: How many σ (sigma) bonds are there in one molecule of propenenitrile, CH₂=CH–C≡N?
items.why:
Students count bonds as lines in the Lewis formula and use 'σ bond' as another name for 'bond'. For each pair of bonded atoms count one σ bond; each additional bond between the same pair is a π bond.

Working: σ bonds: C–H × 3 = 3; C=C contributes 1 σ; C–C contributes 1 σ; C≡N contributes 1 σ. Total = 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6 σ bonds (π bonds: 1 in C=C + 2 in C≡N = 3).
items.specStatementText: Sigma bonds σ form by the head-on combination of atomic orbitals where the electron density is concentrated along the bond axis. Pi bonds π form by the lateral combination of p-orbitals where the electron density is concentrated on opposite sides of the bond axis.
items.working: σ bonds: C–H × 3 = 3; C=C contributes 1 σ; C–C contributes 1 σ; C≡N contributes 1 σ. Total = 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6 σ bonds (π bonds: 1 in C=C + 2 in C≡N = 3).

items.q: Carbon dioxide has the Lewis formula O=C=O. How many σ and π bonds does one CO₂ molecule contain?
items.correct: Two σ bonds and two π bonds
items.misconception: No σ bond and four π bonds
items.why: Students learn 'σ for single bonds, π for multiple bonds' as a slogan and apply it to every shared pair in the multiple bond. Every bonded pair of atoms has exactly one σ bond along the axis; any extra shared pairs are π bonds above and below it.
items.specStatementText: Sigma bonds σ form by the head-on combination of atomic orbitals where the electron density is concentrated along the bond axis. Pi bonds π form by the lateral combination of p-orbitals where the electron density is concentrated on opposite sides of the bond axis.
items.random_wrong: Four σ bonds and zero π bonds

items.q: In ethanenitrile, CH₃CN, the nitrogen atom is joined to carbon by a triple bond and carries one lone pair. What is the hybridization of the nitrogen atom?
items.correct: sp, as it has two electron domains: the triple bond and the lone pair
items.misconception: sp², as it forms three bonds to the carbon atom, one for each shared pair
items.why: Students first meet sp³ in methane, where the number of bonds and the number of domains are both four, and generalize from bonds. Count electron domains around the atom: lone pairs plus bonded atoms. Two domains sp, three sp², four sp³.
items.specStatementText: Hybridization is the concept of mixing atomic orbitals to form new hybrid orbitals for bonding.
items.random_wrong: sp³, as nitrogen is sp³ hybridized in ammonia and keeps that in its compounds

items.q: Which statement about hybridization in an inorganic species is correct?
items.correct: The boron atom in BF₃ is sp² hybridized, with its three hybrid orbitals at 120°
items.misconception: The nitrogen atom in NH₃ is not hybridized, as only carbon forms hybrid orbitals
items.why: Hybridization is usually introduced with organic molecules (methane, ethene, ethyne), so students associate it only with carbon. Apply the same method to any atom: count its electron domains and match them to sp, sp² or sp³.
items.specStatementText: Hybridization is the concept of mixing atomic orbitals to form new hybrid orbitals for bonding.
items.random_wrong: The carbon atom in CO₂ is sp³ hybridized, as it forms 4 bonds in total

items.q: Silicon is a shiny grey solid that melts at 1414 °C, conducts electricity only slightly and does not dissolve in water or in hexane. Which describes the structure of solid silicon?
items.correct: A network in which each Si atom is covalently bonded to four others, as in diamond
items.misconception: A lattice of positive Si ions in a sea of delocalized electrons, as in metals
items.why: Students judge bonding from appearance and conductivity, the everyday signs of a metal, and silicon is sometimes loosely called a 'metalloid'. Identify the bonding from the structure: each Si atom forms four covalent bonds to other Si atoms, and each C atom in graphite forms three covalent bonds. There is no lattice of positive ions in a sea of electrons.
items.specStatementText: Carbon and silicon form covalent network structures.
items.random_wrong: Separate silicon molecules held together by strong intermolecular forces

items.q: C₆₀ fullerene dissolves in methylbenzene, but diamond and graphite do not dissolve in any common solvent. Which statement explains the difference?
items.correct: C₆₀ consists of separate molecules held by London forces; diamond and graphite are covalent networks
items.misconception: C₆₀ splits into ions in methylbenzene, but diamond and graphite cannot form ions
items.why: Dissolving is first met with salts, where the ions separate, and 'dissociation' and 'dissolving' are used almost interchangeably. Distinguish dissolving from ionizing. Most soluble covalent substances (ethanol, glucose) dissolve as molecules held among water molecules by hydrogen bonds.
items.specStatementText: Carbon and silicon form covalent network structures.
items.random_wrong: Diamond and graphite are held together by strong intermolecular forces between their atoms

items.q: In methanamine, CH₃NH₂, the nitrogen atom is sp³ hybridized and carries one lone pair. What is the molecular geometry around the nitrogen atom?
items.correct: Trigonal pyramidal, as the lone pair fills one of the four sp³ orbitals
items.misconception: Bent, as an sp³ atom with a lone pair is bent, like O in water
items.why: Water is the first and most familiar molecule with lone pairs on its central atom, so its shape name, 'bent', becomes attached to 'has a lone pair' rather than to the number of bonded atoms. Count the bonded atoms and lone pairs separately: four sp³ domains with one lone pair give trigonal pyramidal; with two lone pairs, bent.
items.specStatementText: Hybridization is the concept of mixing atomic orbitals to form new hybrid orbitals for bonding.
items.random_wrong: Tetrahedral, as its four sp³ orbitals point to the corners of a tetrahedron

items.q: In the Lewis formula of methanal, H₂CO, the carbon atom is bonded to both H atoms and to the O atom. How many lone pairs are on the oxygen atom?
items.correct: 2 lone pairs, as 4 of the 12 valence electrons remain after the C–H and C=O bonds
items.misconception: 4 lone pairs, as O gains two electrons from C and is an O²⁻ ion with an octet
items.why:
Students often meet ionic bonding first and learn that bonding is 'electrostatic attraction between opposite charges'; they then look for opposite charges in every bond. For HCl, knowing that it forms H⁺ and Cl⁻ in water reinforces the idea that the molecule contains these ions. Keep the models distinct. In HCl gas the molecule contains a shared pair between H and Cl; the bond is polar (partial charges δ+ and δ−) but no ions are present. Ions form only when HCl reacts with water.

Working: Valence electrons: C 4 + 2 × H 1 + O 6 = 12. Carbon forms two C–H bonds (4 electrons) and a C=O double bond (4 electrons), 8 electrons in bonds. The remaining 12 − 8 = 4 electrons form 2 lone pairs on O. Check: O has 4 (C=O) + 4 (lone pairs) = 8; C has 2 × 2 + 4 = 8; each H has 2.
items.specStatementText: A covalent bond is formed by the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positively charged nuclei. The octet rule refers to the tendency of atoms to gain a valence shell with a total of 8 electrons.
items.random_wrong: 3 lone pairs, as the C=O double bond is one shared pair, so O needs three more
items.working: Valence electrons: C 4 + 2 × H 1 + O 6 = 12. Carbon forms two C–H bonds (4 electrons) and a C=O double bond (4 electrons), 8 electrons in bonds. The remaining 12 − 8 = 4 electrons form 2 lone pairs on O. Check: O has 4 (C=O) + 4 (lone pairs) = 8; C has 2 × 2 + 4 = 8; each H has 2.

items.q: The O–O bond in hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂, has a length of 148 pm; the O=O bond in oxygen, O₂, has a length of 121 pm. Which statement about the strengths of these two bonds is correct?
items.correct: O=O is stronger, as two shared pairs attract both nuclei more than one
items.misconception: O=O is weaker, as the two shared pairs between the nuclei repel each other strongly
items.why: Students have learned (in VSEPR) that electron pairs repel, and apply this to the pairs within one bond, without weighing it against the attraction of those pairs to the nuclei. Compare the data: bond length falls and bond enthalpy rises from C–C to C=C to C≡C. The net effect of more shared pairs is a stronger attraction between the nuclei and the shared electrons.
items.specStatementText: Single, double and triple bonds involve one, two and three shared pairs of electrons respectively.
items.random_wrong: O=O is weaker, as oxygen reacts so readily, for example in combustion reactions

items.q: Ammonia, NH₃, reacts with a hydrogen ion, H⁺, to form the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺. Which statement about the bonds in NH₄⁺ is correct?
items.correct: All four N–H bonds are identical, although one formed from the lone pair on nitrogen
items.misconception: The bond formed from the lone pair on nitrogen is longer and weaker than the other three N–H bonds
items.why: Lewis formulas often draw the coordination bond with an arrow, which makes it look like a different kind of bond, and the history of the pair's origin is taken as a lasting property. The arrow records only where the electrons came from. Electrons are indistinguishable, so after the bond forms all four N–H bonds are equivalent.
items.specStatementText: A coordination bond is a covalent bond in which both the electrons of the shared pair originate from the same atom.
items.random_wrong: The new bond formed from a pair of electrons supplied by the H⁺ ion to nitrogen

items.q: Electronegativity values: H 2.2, N 3.0. Which statement describes the N–H bond in ammonia, NH₃?
items.correct: The shared pair lies closer to nitrogen, so nitrogen is δ− and hydrogen is δ+
items.misconception: Both atoms gain a share of the pair, so nitrogen and hydrogen are both δ−
items.why: Introductory descriptions say that each atom 'gains a share' of the electrons to complete its shell, and the shared pair is counted in both atoms' octets, so students picture both atoms as having gained negative charge. Partial charges come from unequal sharing, not from sharing itself: electron density shifts towards one atom (δ−) and away from the other (δ+), and the two partial charges sum to zero.
items.specStatementText: Bond polarity results from the difference in electronegativities of the bonded atoms.
items.random_wrong: Each hydrogen atom has given its electron to nitrogen, so N³⁻ and H⁺ ions attract

items.q: The diagram shows a student's Lewis formula for ammonia, NH₃, with each shared pair drawn as one dot and one cross. What is wrong with it?
items.correct: The lone pair on nitrogen is missing, so nitrogen is shown with only six electrons
items.misconception: Nothing: nitrogen forms three bonds, and its three shared pairs complete its valence shell
items.why: Structural formulas and displayed formulas omit lone pairs, so students who move from them to Lewis formulas count only the bond lines around an atom. A Lewis formula shows ALL valence electrons. Count both bonding pairs and lone pairs: N in NCl₃ has 3 × 2 + 2 = 8 electrons, a complete octet.
items.specStatementText: A covalent bond is formed by the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positively charged nuclei. The octet rule refers to the tendency of atoms to gain a valence shell with a total of 8 electrons.
items.random_wrong: Each hydrogen atom should also have three lone pairs, so that every atom has eight electrons

items.q: The diagram shows the Lewis formulas of beryllium chloride, BeCl₂, and dichlorine monoxide, Cl₂O, each drawn with its three atoms in a straight line. Which deduction about the molecular geometry of Cl₂O is correct?
items.correct: Cl₂O is bent, because the two lone pairs on oxygen repel its two bonds out of a straight line
items.misconception: Cl₂O is linear, because its Lewis formula shows the Cl–O–Cl bond angle as 180°
items.why: Lewis formulas are conventionally drawn with pairs on four sides of the atom (above, below, left, right), which looks like a cross with 90° angles, and students take the drawing as a picture of the molecule. Use VSEPR to predict angles in three dimensions. Four domains around an atom point towards the corners of a tetrahedron, 109.5° apart, not the corners of a square.
items.specStatementText: The valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) model enables the shapes of molecules to be predicted from the repulsion of electron domains around a central atom.
items.random_wrong: Cl₂O is linear, because only the two bonding pairs on oxygen affect its shape

items.q: The diagram shows a molecule of trichloromethane, CHCl₃, drawn with wedge and dash bonds; the arrows show the three C–Cl bond dipoles (electronegativity: H 2.2, C 2.6, Cl 3.2). Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The molecule is polar, because its three C–Cl dipoles add to give a net dipole towards Cl
items.misconception: The molecule is polar, but only because of the C–H bond, since the three C–Cl dipoles cancel each other
items.why: BF₃ and BCl₃ are the standard examples of bond dipoles cancelling, and students remember 'three identical bonds cancel' without the condition that the three bonds must be trigonal planar. Add the bond dipoles as vectors in the actual geometry. Three equal dipoles cancel only in a trigonal planar arrangement; in a tetrahedral or trigonal pyramidal arrangement they leave a resultant.
items.specStatementText: Molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity and molecular geometry.
items.random_wrong: The molecule is non-polar, because it carries no overall charge, so its charges must balance out

items.q: The graph shows the boiling points of the hydrogen halides HF, HCl, HBr and HI plotted against molar mass. Which statement is supported by the graph?
items.correct: London forces between HI molecules are stronger than those between HCl molecules, because HI has more electrons
items.misconception: The rise in boiling point from HCl to HI is due to dipole–dipole forces, which strengthen as the molecules get larger
items.why: London forces are introduced as 'the forces between non-polar molecules' and are often the only force listed for them, so students treat them as exclusive to non-polar substances. List forces cumulatively: every molecule has London forces; polar molecules also have dipole–dipole forces; molecules with H on N, O or F also have hydrogen bonding.
items.specStatementText: Given comparable molar mass, the relative strengths of intermolecular forces are generally: London (dispersion) forces < dipole–dipole forces < hydrogen bonding.
items.random_wrong: Hydrogen bonds between HCl molecules are weaker than those between HF molecules, so HCl boils lower

items.q: The diagram shows a paper chromatogram with a scale in cm measured from the bottom edge of the paper. What is the RF value of spot X?
items.why:
The bottom of the paper is the most obvious reference point, and the baseline is a faint pencil line that students forget is the true starting point. Measure from the baseline: distance moved = position of spot centre (or front) − position of baseline.

Working: From the scale: baseline at 1.0 cm, solvent front at 9.0 cm, centre of spot X at 7.0 cm. Distance moved by X = 7.0 − 1.0 = 6.0 cm. Distance moved by solvent = 9.0 − 1.0 = 8.0 cm. RF = 6.0 cm ÷ 8.0 cm = 0.75 (no units).
items.specStatementText: Chromatography is a technique used to separate the components of a mixture based on their relative attractions involving intermolecular forces to mobile and stationary phases.

items.q: The diagram shows two structures, P and Q, drawn for the nitrite ion, NO₂⁻, linked by a double-headed arrow. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: P and Q are resonance structures, differing only in the positions of electrons; every nitrite ion is one hybrid of both
items.misconception: Each nitrite ion oscillates between P and Q, its double bond moving from one oxygen atom to the other
items.why: The double-headed arrow between resonance structures looks like the arrow for a reaction or an equilibrium, and the word 'resonance' suggests oscillation. Think of the resonance structures as imperfect drawings of one real structure. No single Lewis formula can show delocalized electrons, so several are drawn.
items.specStatementText: Resonance structures occur when there is more than one possible position for a double bond in a molecule.
items.random_wrong: A sample of sodium nitrite contains ions of structure P and ions of structure Q in equal numbers

items.q: The diagram shows the bonding between the two carbon atoms in ethene, C₂H₄, with the C–C line representing the σ bond. Which statement describes the bond labelled X?
items.correct: A π bond: the two p orbitals overlap sideways, giving electron density on both sides of the axis
items.misconception: A π bond formed by head-on overlap of an sp² hybrid orbital from each carbon atom
items.why: Students picture hybridization as preparing all the orbitals for bonding, so they assume every bond uses a hybrid orbital. Remember what is left over: sp leaves two p orbitals, sp² leaves one. Those p orbitals overlap sideways to form π bonds.
items.specStatementText: Sigma bonds σ form by the head-on combination of atomic orbitals where the electron density is concentrated along the bond axis. Pi bonds π form by the lateral combination of p-orbitals where the electron density is concentrated on opposite sides of the bond axis.
items.random_wrong: A second σ bond, because every shared pair between the two carbon atoms must be a σ bond

items.q: The diagram shows the Lewis formula of bromine pentafluoride, BrF₅, with the atoms drawn flat on the page. What is the molecular geometry of BrF₅?
items.correct: Square pyramidal, as one of the six octahedral positions holds the lone pair
items.misconception: Octahedral, as the five bonding pairs and the lone pair make six electron domains
items.why: Students correctly learn that lone pairs count when arranging electron domains and then use that arrangement as the name of the shape, not realizing that the shape is named from the atoms. Two steps: arrange all domains (electron-domain geometry), then describe where the atoms are (molecular geometry). Lone pairs influence the shape but are not part of its name.
items.specStatementText: Some atoms can form molecules in which they have an expanded octet of electrons.
items.random_wrong: Trigonal bipyramidal, as only the five bonding pairs repel one another

items.q: Is a covalent bond a physical object, such as the shared electrons acting as a stick or link between atoms?
items.correct: No. The bond is the attraction between the shared electron pair and both nuclei. The electrons are not a rigid link; they are the negative charge that both nuclei attract.
items.misconception: The shared pair of electrons is itself the bond, a material link holding the atoms together like a stick or a hook.
items.why: Ball-and-stick models and line drawings represent every bond as a physical rod or a line, and the phrase 'a bond is a shared pair' is easily read as 'a bond is a thing made of electrons'. A line in a formula stands for a shared pair, but the bonding is the electrostatic attraction between that pair and the two nuclei. Without the attraction to both nuclei there is no bond.
items.specStatementText: A covalent bond is formed by the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positively charged nuclei. The octet rule refers to the tendency of atoms to gain a valence shell with a total of 8 electrons.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a double bond count as one shared pair of electrons when counting electrons around an atom?
items.correct: No. A double bond is two shared pairs (four electrons) and a triple bond is three shared pairs (six electrons).
items.misconception: Each bond line between two atoms, including a double bond, counts as one shared pair of electrons.
items.why: Students learn 'one bond = one shared pair' for single bonds and apply it to every connection between two atoms, so a double bond is counted as one bond and one pair. Count the lines: each line in a Lewis formula is one shared pair. Each carbon in C₂H₄ has two C–H pairs and two pairs in C=C, so eight electrons.
items.specStatementText: A covalent bond is formed by the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positively charged nuclei. The octet rule refers to the tendency of atoms to gain a valence shell with a total of 8 electrons.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the positive charge of NH₄⁺ mean that its nitrogen atom has lost an electron and so has fewer than eight?
items.correct: No. The charge belongs to the whole ion: it has one fewer electron than the total valence electrons of the neutral atoms (5 + 4 × 1 − 1 = 8). In the Lewis formula nitrogen has four bonding pairs, a full octet.
items.misconception: The charge of a polyatomic ion sits on its central atom, so in a positive ion the central atom has lost an electron from its octet.
items.why: Students first meet charge as a property of single-atom ions (Na⁺, Cl⁻), where the charge does belong to one atom, and transfer this to polyatomic ions, often helped by formulas that print the charge next to the central atom. Count the electrons for the whole ion: add the valence electrons of all atoms and adjust by the charge, then distribute them. For NH₄⁺, eight electrons form four N–H bonding pairs.
items.specStatementText: A covalent bond is formed by the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positively charged nuclei. The octet rule refers to the tendency of atoms to gain a valence shell with a total of 8 electrons.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a C=C or C≡C bond weaker than a C–C single bond because alkenes and alkynes are more reactive than alkanes?
items.correct: No. Multiple bonds are stronger overall: average bond enthalpies are C–C 346, C=C 614 and C≡C 839 kJ mol⁻¹. Addition does not break the whole double bond: it converts C=C into C–C, which needs only about 614 − 346 = 268 kJ mol⁻¹, less than a C–C single bond. That, and the electron-rich double bond attracting electrophiles, is why alkenes react readily; the bond as a whole is not weaker.
items.misconception: Alkenes and alkynes react more readily than alkanes, so their multiple bonds must be weaker than single bonds.
items.why: Students connect reactivity directly with bond weakness, and they see alkenes undergo addition easily while alkanes are unreactive. Separate the strength of the whole bond from the energy needed to convert it into a single bond. A C=C bond (614 kJ mol⁻¹) is stronger than C–C (346 kJ mol⁻¹), but converting C=C into C–C, which is all that addition does, needs only about 614 − 346 = 268 kJ mol⁻¹, less than breaking a C–C single bond.
items.specStatementText: Single, double and triple bonds involve one, two and three shared pairs of electrons respectively.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is every compound of a metal and a non-metal ionic?
items.correct: No. Aluminium chloride is covalent: in the vapour it exists as Al₂Cl₆ molecules held together by covalent bonds, including coordination bonds.
items.misconception: A compound of a metal with a non-metal is always ionic, so aluminium chloride consists of Al³⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
items.why: The rule 'metal + non-metal = ionic' is a common simplification in early chemistry courses, and students apply it without exceptions. Treat the metal/non-metal rule as a guide. Aluminium chloride has covalent character; Al₂Cl₆ molecules contain coordination bonds from Cl lone pairs to Al atoms.
items.specStatementText: A coordination bond is a covalent bond in which both the electrons of the shared pair originate from the same atom.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does each atom always supply one electron to every covalent bond?
items.correct: No. In a coordination bond both electrons come from the same atom. This happens when one atom has a lone pair and the other has no electron to share but can accept a pair.
items.misconception: In every covalent bond each atom contributes one electron to the shared pair.
items.why: The first covalent bonds students draw (H₂, Cl₂, CH₄) all form by each atom contributing one electron, and dot-and-cross diagrams reinforce this pattern. Check the electron counts. An Al atom in AlCl₃ has used all three of its valence electrons, so any further bond must be made with a pair supplied entirely by the other atom.
items.specStatementText: A coordination bond is a covalent bond in which both the electrons of the shared pair originate from the same atom.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do lone pairs on an outer (terminal) atom affect the bond angles around the central atom?
items.correct: No. Only the electron domains around the central atom determine its bond angles. The lone pairs on oxygen in H₂CO belong to oxygen and do not count as domains of carbon.
items.misconception: All the lone pairs in a molecule push the bonds together, including lone pairs on outer atoms, so two lone pairs anywhere give an angle of about 104.5°, as in water.
items.why: Students learn that 'lone pairs reduce bond angles' in H₂O and NH₃ and apply it to any lone pair they see in the Lewis formula, without checking which atom holds it. Identify the central atom and count only the domains on it. In H₂CO carbon has three domains (two C–H bonds and C=O), so the angles are close to 120°.
items.specStatementText: The valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) model enables the shapes of molecules to be predicted from the repulsion of electron domains around a central atom.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does electronegativity increase with atomic number, so that a heavier atom attracts the shared pair more strongly?
items.correct: No. Electronegativity increases across a period but decreases down a group, because the shared pair is further from the nucleus and more shielded. P (atomic number 15) has the same electronegativity as H (2.2).
items.misconception: An atom with more protons attracts the shared electrons more strongly, so the larger the difference in atomic number, the more polar the bond.
items.why: Students correctly learn that nuclear charge attracts electrons and apply it on its own, ignoring the effect of distance and shielding, which is harder to picture. Use the electronegativity values given, not atomic numbers. Bond polarity depends on the difference in electronegativity: P–H (2.2, 2.2) is essentially non-polar.
items.specStatementText: Bond polarity results from the difference in electronegativities of the bonded atoms.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the most polar bond the one between the two most electronegative atoms?
items.correct: No. Bond polarity depends on the DIFFERENCE in electronegativity. O–F joins two very electronegative atoms but the difference is only 0.6; C–F has a difference of 1.4 and is more polar.
items.misconception: A bond is more polar the more electronegative its atoms are, so a bond between two highly electronegative atoms is the most polar.
items.why: Students link 'electronegative' with 'polar' and look at the size of the values rather than their difference. Subtract the values. Polarity arises from unequal sharing; two atoms that both attract strongly share the pair more evenly than two atoms of very different electronegativity.
items.specStatementText: Bond polarity results from the difference in electronegativities of the bonded atoms.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a molecule with no overall charge have a dipole moment?
items.correct: Yes. A dipole is a separation of charge within the molecule, not an overall charge. H₂O is neutral but has a net dipole because its δ− and δ+ centres do not coincide.
items.misconception: A molecule with no overall charge cannot have a dipole, because its positive and negative charges cancel.
items.why: Students confuse a dipole (separated partial charges) with a net charge on a particle, as on an ion. Check where the charge lies, not only how much there is. A polar molecule is neutral overall, but one end is δ+ and the other δ−.
items.specStatementText: Molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity and molecular geometry.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a lone pair on the central atom the only source of a net dipole moment?
items.correct: No. Molecular polarity comes from bond dipoles that do not cancel. CH₃Cl has no lone pair on carbon but is polar. Lone pairs matter because they affect the geometry.
items.misconception: Molecules are polar because of lone pairs on the central atom; without a lone pair a molecule is non-polar.
items.why: Explanations of why H₂O and NH₃ are polar mention their lone pairs (which make the shape asymmetric), and students shorten this to 'lone pairs make molecules polar'. Use lone pairs to work out the geometry, then decide whether the bond dipoles cancel in that geometry.
items.specStatementText: Molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity and molecular geometry.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does graphite conduct because its layers can slide?
items.correct: No. Sliding layers explain softness and lubrication. Conduction is due to the electrons delocalized within each layer.
items.misconception: Graphite conducts electricity because its layers slide over one another and carry charge as they move.
items.why: Graphite's two distinctive properties, slipperiness and conductivity, are taught together from the same layer diagram, so students merge the explanations. Match each property to its cause: weak London forces between layers make graphite soft; delocalized electrons within layers make it conduct.
items.specStatementText: Carbon and silicon form covalent network structures.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are all allotropes of carbon giant covalent networks?
items.correct: No. Fullerenes such as C₆₀ are molecular: separate C₆₀ molecules are held together by London forces, so C₆₀ sublimes at a much lower temperature than diamond or graphite and dissolves in non-polar solvents such as methylbenzene.
items.misconception: Every form of carbon is a giant covalent structure like diamond and graphite, with very high melting points and insolubility in all solvents.
items.why: Diamond and graphite are taught as the standard carbon allotropes, and students extend their properties to every form of carbon. Classify each allotrope by its structure. C₆₀ is a discrete molecule of 60 atoms, so its physical properties are those of a simple molecular substance.
items.specStatementText: Carbon and silicon form covalent network structures.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do all allotropes of an element share the same properties because they are made of the same atoms?
items.correct: No. Allotropes have different bonding and structural patterns, so they have different physical and chemical properties. Graphite conducts electricity; diamond does not.
items.misconception: Allotropes of carbon are all made of carbon atoms, so if graphite conducts electricity, diamond must conduct too.
items.why: Students often attribute the properties of a substance to its atoms rather than to its structure, so they expect substances made of the same element to behave alike. Explain each property from the structure. In graphite each C atom has one delocalized electron; in diamond all four valence electrons are in localized C–C bonds, so diamond has no mobile charge carriers.
items.specStatementText: Carbon and silicon form covalent network structures.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a very high melting point show that a substance is ionic?
items.correct: No. Covalent network substances such as silicon dioxide and diamond also have very high melting points, because melting them breaks strong covalent bonds.
items.misconception: Any compound with a very high melting point, such as a high-melting oxide, must be ionic.
items.why: High melting points are first taught as a property of ionic compounds, and many familiar high-melting oxides (MgO, CaO) are ionic. Do not infer bonding from melting point alone. SiO₂ is a covalent network: each Si atom is bonded to four O atoms and each O to two Si atoms.
items.specStatementText: Carbon and silicon form covalent network structures.

items.q: Does the term 'van der Waals forces' mean London (dispersion) forces only?
items.correct: No. In the IB guide, van der Waals forces is the inclusive term for dipole–dipole, dipole–induced dipole and London (dispersion) forces.
items.misconception: Van der Waals forces are the same thing as London (dispersion) forces, the weak forces between non-polar molecules.
items.why: Many textbooks and older courses use 'van der Waals forces' to mean only the forces between non-polar molecules, so students learn the two terms as synonyms. Use 'van der Waals forces' for all three: London, dipole–induced dipole and dipole–dipole. Hydrogen bonding is named separately.
items.specStatementText: The nature of the force that exists between molecules is determined by the size and polarity of the molecules. Intermolecular forces include London (dispersion), dipole-induced dipole, dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding.

items.q: Does a polar molecule take part in dipole–dipole forces with any neighbouring molecule?
items.correct: No. Dipole–dipole forces need a permanent dipole on BOTH molecules. Between a polar and a non-polar molecule the force is dipole–induced dipole.
items.misconception: If one of two molecules is polar, the force between them is dipole–dipole.
items.why: Students identify a polar molecule and attach 'dipole–dipole' to it as a label, without checking the partner molecule. Name the force from both partners: permanent dipole + permanent dipole = dipole–dipole; permanent dipole + non-polar = dipole–induced dipole.
items.specStatementText: The nature of the force that exists between molecules is determined by the size and polarity of the molecules. Intermolecular forces include London (dispersion), dipole-induced dipole, dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding.

items.q: Is a hydrogen bond a bond between two hydrogen atoms?
items.correct: No. A hydrogen bond links an H atom to an electronegative atom (N, O or F) with a lone pair in another molecule. Two H atoms are both δ+ and repel.
items.misconception: A hydrogen bond is an attraction between the hydrogen atoms of neighbouring molecules.
items.why: The name suggests a bond between hydrogens, by analogy with 'carbon–carbon bond'. Think about charges: H on O is δ+, so it is attracted to a δ− atom with a lone pair, not to another δ+ hydrogen.
items.specStatementText: The nature of the force that exists between molecules is determined by the size and polarity of the molecules. Intermolecular forces include London (dispersion), dipole-induced dipole, dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding.

items.q: Does the compound with the longest carbon chain always have the highest boiling point?
items.correct: No. Chain length raises boiling point within a homologous series. Between different families of comparable molar mass, the type of intermolecular force matters more: propane (3 C) boils far lower than ethanol (2 C).
items.misconception: Boiling point rises with the number of carbon atoms, so a three-carbon compound boils higher than any two-carbon compound.
items.why: The rule 'boiling point increases with chain length' is learned for homologous series and applied across different series. Apply the chain-length trend only within one homologous series. Across series of comparable molar mass, use the type of intermolecular force.
items.specStatementText: Given comparable molar mass, the relative strengths of intermolecular forces are generally: London (dispersion) forces < dipole–dipole forces < hydrogen bonding.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the shared electrons in covalent bonds free to move through a substance?
items.correct: No. In a simple molecular substance the bonding electrons are localized between two particular nuclei, and the lone pairs are held by particular atoms, so they cannot carry a current. Only delocalized electrons, as in graphite and metals, are mobile.
items.misconception: The shared electrons in covalent bonds move between atoms, so covalent substances can conduct through them.
items.why: 'Sharing' suggests movement back and forth between atoms, and students know that electrons carry current in metals. Distinguish localized shared pairs (fixed between two nuclei) from delocalized electrons (spread over many atoms). Only delocalized electrons conduct.
items.specStatementText: Given comparable molar mass, the relative strengths of intermolecular forces are generally: London (dispersion) forces < dipole–dipole forces < hydrogen bonding.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a liquid insoluble in water because it is less dense and floats?
items.correct: No. Density decides which layer is on top once two liquids fail to mix; it does not decide whether they mix. Ethanol is also less dense than water but mixes with it completely.
items.misconception: Hexane does not dissolve in water because it is less dense and floats on top.
items.why: Everyday experience of oil floating on water links 'floating' with 'not mixing'. Explain solubility by the forces between particles: hexane cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, so it cannot replace the hydrogen bonds it would break between water molecules.
items.specStatementText: Given comparable molar mass, the relative strengths of intermolecular forces are generally: London (dispersion) forces < dipole–dipole forces < hydrogen bonding.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a substance dissolve only if its particles are small enough to fit into gaps between water molecules?
items.correct: No. Solubility depends on the attractions between solute and solvent molecules, not on fitting into spaces. Large molecules such as sucrose are very soluble in water because they form many hydrogen bonds with it.
items.misconception: Substances dissolve when their particles fit into the spaces between the solvent's particles, so large molecules cannot dissolve.
items.why: The 'particles fill the gaps' picture is used to explain why volumes do not simply add on mixing, and students turn it into an explanation of solubility. Use intermolecular forces: a solute dissolves when it can form attractions with the solvent comparable to those broken.
items.specStatementText: Given comparable molar mass, the relative strengths of intermolecular forces are generally: London (dispersion) forces < dipole–dipole forces < hydrogen bonding.

items.q: Does the retardation factor measure how far the spot has fallen behind the solvent front?
items.correct: No. RF is the fraction of the solvent's distance that the spot travelled: distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent, both from the baseline.
items.misconception: RF measures the retardation of the spot: the distance between the spot and the solvent front divided by the distance moved by the solvent.
items.why: The name 'retardation factor' suggests a measure of how much the component was held back, so students measure the gap between the spot and the front. Despite its name, RF is calculated from the distance the spot moved forward from the baseline, not from the distance it lags behind.
items.specStatementText: Chromatography is a technique used to separate the components of a mixture based on their relative attractions involving intermolecular forces to mobile and stationary phases.

items.q: Does a component's RF value increase if the solvent is left to run for longer?
items.correct: No. Both distances increase in the same proportion, so RF stays constant for a given stationary phase, solvent and temperature. That is why RF values can be used to identify components.
items.misconception: The longer the chromatogram runs, the further every spot travels, so a component with a low RF would reach a higher RF given more time.
items.why: Students focus on the distance a spot travels, which does increase with time, and forget that RF is a ratio to the distance the solvent travels. RF is a ratio of two distances that grow together, so it is characteristic of the component under the stated conditions.
items.specStatementText: Chromatography is a technique used to separate the components of a mixture based on their relative attractions involving intermolecular forces to mobile and stationary phases.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a component's RF depend only on its solubility in the solvent?
items.correct: No. It depends on the balance between the component's attraction to the mobile phase and its attraction to the stationary phase. Both phases matter.
items.misconception: Only solubility in the solvent matters: the more soluble component travels further, and the paper plays no part in the separation.
items.why: Simple accounts explain chromatography as 'more soluble substances travel further', with no mention of the stationary phase. Describe separation as a competition: a component spends time attracted to the stationary phase and time carried by the mobile phase, and the balance decides its RF.
items.specStatementText: Chromatography is a technique used to separate the components of a mixture based on their relative attractions involving intermolecular forces to mobile and stationary phases.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a sample of a species with resonance a mixture of different molecules or ions, one for each resonance structure?
items.correct: No. Every molecule or ion in the sample is the same resonance hybrid.
items.misconception: A sample contains a mixture of species, each having the structure of one of the resonance structures, in equal amounts.
items.why: Students explain the equal average bond lengths by averaging over a population of different particles, as they would for a mixture of isomers. Each individual ion already has identical bonds; the equality is a property of every particle, not an average over a mixture.
items.specStatementText: Resonance structures occur when there is more than one possible position for a double bond in a molecule.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can the number of C=C bonds in benzene be found by dividing its enthalpy change of hydrogenation by that of cyclohexene?
items.correct: No. That assumes benzene has isolated C=C bonds like cyclohexene. The smaller value shows that benzene is stabilized by delocalization; it still adds three moles of H₂ to form cyclohexane.
items.misconception: The enthalpy change of hydrogenation is always proportional to the number of C=C bonds, so a value between one and two times that of cyclohexene means the molecule has only one or two C=C bonds.
items.why: Students apply a proportional pattern that holds for molecules with isolated double bonds and read a smaller value as fewer bonds. Compare the reactions directly: benzene + 3H₂ → cyclohexane. It adds three moles of H₂, but it is about 152 kJ mol⁻¹ lower in energy than a structure with three isolated C=C bonds.
items.specStatementText: Benzene, C₆H₆, is an important example of a molecule that has resonance.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is an enthalpy change smaller because the reaction does not go to completion?
items.correct: No. ΔH is quoted per mole of reaction as written, so it does not depend on how much reacts in a particular experiment.
items.misconception: A less exothermic value means that less of the substance reacted, so less energy was released per mole.
items.why: Students connect ΔH with the heat measured in their own experiments, where incomplete reaction does reduce the heat released. ΔH refers to one mole of reaction as written. A less exothermic ΔH for benzene reflects its lower starting energy, not incomplete reaction.
items.specStatementText: Benzene, C₆H₆, is an important example of a molecule that has resonance.
