items.q: Can period 2 atoms such as C, N and O expand their octet?
items.correct: No. Period 2 atoms have only 2s and 2p orbitals in their valence shell, which hold at most eight electrons. Expanded octets occur for atoms of period 3 onwards (P, S, Cl, Xe).
items.misconception: Any central atom can have more than eight electrons if that gives more double bonds, including C, N and O.
items.why: Students meet expanded octets for S and P and apply the idea to any central atom, especially when it lets them draw a structure with equal bonds. Check the period of the central atom before drawing more than four electron pairs around it. N in NO₃⁻ and O in O₃ are limited to eight electrons.
items.specStatementText: Some atoms can form molecules in which they have an expanded octet of electrons.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do lone pairs occupy axial positions in a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement?
items.correct: No. Lone pairs occupy equatorial positions, where they have only two neighbours at 90° instead of three, which minimizes repulsion. SF₄ is therefore see-saw and ClF₃ T-shaped.
items.misconception: Lone pairs go into axial positions, at the top and bottom of the trigonal bipyramid, where they are out of the way.
items.why: Diagrams of trigonal bipyramids draw the axial positions as the most isolated-looking ones, and students do not count the 90° interactions. Count the 90° interactions: an axial position has three neighbours at 90°, an equatorial position only two. Lone pairs take the positions with fewer 90° neighbours.
items.specStatementText: Some atoms can form molecules in which they have an expanded octet of electrons.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are all bonding electrons around an atom assigned to it when calculating formal charge?
items.correct: No. Only half of the bonding electrons are assigned to each atom, because each bonding pair is shared equally between two atoms: FC = V − N − ½B.
items.misconception: In the formal charge calculation all the bonding electrons around an atom are subtracted, not half of them.
items.why: When checking octets, students count every bonding electron around an atom, and they carry this count into the formal charge formula. Remember what formal charge assumes: equal sharing. Each atom owns one electron from each bonding pair.
items.specStatementText: Formal charge values can be calculated for each atom in a species and used to determine which of several possible Lewis formulas is preferred.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is formal charge the same as oxidation state?
items.correct: No. Oxidation state assigns all bonding electrons to the more electronegative atom; formal charge shares them equally. In CO, carbon has oxidation state +2 but formal charge −1.
items.misconception: Formal charge and oxidation state are the same number, so the formal charge on an atom equals its oxidation state.
items.why: Both are hypothetical charges written on atoms and both are calculated by electron bookkeeping, so students use them interchangeably. Choose the rule for the purpose: oxidation state (electrons to the more electronegative atom) for redox; formal charge (equal sharing) for choosing between Lewis formulas.
items.specStatementText: Formal charge values can be calculated for each atom in a species and used to determine which of several possible Lewis formulas is preferred.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If every atom has an octet in two Lewis formulas, are they equally good?
items.correct: No. Both may obey the octet rule, but the preferred formula is the one with formal charges closest to zero. For CO₂, O=C=O is preferred to O≡C–O.
items.misconception: Any Lewis formula in which every atom has an octet is correct, so there is no reason to prefer one over another.
items.why: The octet rule is the main test students apply to Lewis formulas, so once it is satisfied they see no need for a further criterion. After checking octets, calculate formal charges and choose the formula with formal charges closest to zero.
items.specStatementText: Formal charge values can be calculated for each atom in a species and used to determine which of several possible Lewis formulas is preferred.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the Lewis formula with a negative formal charge on the most electronegative atom always preferred?
items.correct: No. The first criterion is formal charges as close to zero as possible. Placing a negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom only decides between formulas that cannot avoid formal charges.
items.misconception: The preferred Lewis formula is the one that places a negative formal charge on the most electronegative atom.
items.why: Students remember the electronegativity rule because it involves reasoning, and forget that it is a tie-breaker that comes second. Apply the criteria in order: first, formal charges closest to zero; only then, negative charge on the more electronegative atom.
items.specStatementText: Formal charge values can be calculated for each atom in a species and used to determine which of several possible Lewis formulas is preferred.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the Lewis formula containing the strongest individual bond (for example a triple bond) the preferred one?
items.correct: No. A triple bond in one formula comes with a single bond elsewhere, and the preference is decided by formal charge, not by the strength of any one bond.
items.misconception: The Lewis formula containing a triple bond is preferred, because a triple bond is stronger and makes the molecule more stable.
items.why: Students know that triple bonds are strong and assume that including the strongest possible bond gives the most stable structure. Compare formulas using formal charges; for CO₂ the formula with two double bonds and all formal charges zero is preferred.
items.specStatementText: Formal charge values can be calculated for each atom in a species and used to determine which of several possible Lewis formulas is preferred.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a triple bond made of two σ bonds and one π bond?
items.correct: No. A triple bond is one σ bond and two π bonds. Only one head-on overlap is possible along the bond axis; the two further bonds form by lateral overlap of two pairs of p orbitals.
items.misconception: A triple bond contains two σ bonds and one π bond.
items.why: Students remember that a double bond is 'one of each' and build the triple bond by adding another σ bond. Only one σ bond can lie along the axis between two nuclei. The second and third bonds use the two p orbitals at right angles to the axis, giving two π bonds.
items.specStatementText: Sigma bonds σ form by the head-on combination of atomic orbitals where the electron density is concentrated along the bond axis. Pi bonds π form by the lateral combination of p-orbitals where the electron density is concentrated on opposite sides of the bond axis.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does an element always have the same hybridization in all its compounds?
items.correct: No. Hybridization depends on the number of electron domains around the atom in that species. Nitrogen is sp³ in NH₃ but sp in HCN; carbon is sp³ in CH₄, sp² in ethene and sp in ethyne.
items.misconception: Each element has its own characteristic hybridization (carbon sp³, nitrogen sp³ as in NH₃) which it keeps in all molecules.
items.why: Students first meet each element's hybridization in one familiar molecule and attach it to the element. Work out the hybridization afresh for each atom in each species by counting its electron domains.
items.specStatementText: Hybridization is the concept of mixing atomic orbitals to form new hybrid orbitals for bonding.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In a Lewis formula, is the number of electrons in an atom's valence shell the same as the number of valence electrons of the free atom?
items.correct: No. Both electrons of every shared pair count towards the valence shell of each bonded atom, so the count includes electrons supplied by the partner atoms. Boron has three valence electrons, but in BCl₃ its valence shell holds six.
items.misconception: The number of electrons in an atom's valence shell in a molecule equals the number of valence electrons of the free atom.
items.why: Students learn 'boron has three valence electrons' and 'chlorine has seven' as fixed properties of each element, and the same phrase 'valence electrons' is used both for the free atom and for the electrons around an atom in a Lewis formula. Count both electrons of every bonding pair around the atom, plus its lone pairs.
items.specStatementText: A covalent bond is formed by the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positively charged nuclei. The octet rule refers to the tendency of atoms to gain a valence shell with a total of 8 electrons.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does HCl form hydrogen bonds, since its H atom is covalently bonded to an electronegative atom?
items.correct: No. Hydrogen bonding involves H covalently bonded to N, O or F, attracted to a lone pair on an N, O or F atom of a neighbouring molecule. HCl molecules are held by dipole–dipole and London forces.
items.misconception: A hydrogen bond forms whenever hydrogen is covalently bonded to any electronegative atom, including chlorine.
items.why: The general statement 'hydrogen, covalently bonded to an electronegative atom' does not name N, O and F, and chlorine's electronegativity (3.2) is higher than nitrogen's (3.0), so students extend hydrogen bonding to HCl. Look for H bonded to N, O or F as the donor and an N, O or F lone pair as the acceptor; other polar H–X bonds give dipole–dipole forces.
items.specStatementText: The nature of the force that exists between molecules is determined by the size and polarity of the molecules. Intermolecular forces include London (dispersion), dipole-induced dipole, dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does benzene resist addition because its C=C double bonds are stronger than those in alkenes?
items.correct: No. Benzene has no localized C=C bonds: its six C–C bonds are identical and intermediate between single and double. It resists addition because addition would destroy the extra stability of its delocalized π system.
items.misconception: Benzene contains three localized C=C bonds that are unusually strong, and their strength is why it does not undergo addition.
items.why: Students keep the Kekulé picture of three fixed C=C bonds, then hear that benzene is 'very stable' and resists addition. They reconcile the two by equating stability with the strength of individual bonds rather than with delocalization over the ring. Attribute benzene's stability, and its preference for substitution, to delocalization of the π electrons over the whole ring, not to strong individual double bonds.
items.specStatementText: Benzene, C₆H₆, is an important example of a molecule that has resonance.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a resonance structure be drawn by moving an atom, such as H, to a different position?
items.correct: No. The resonance structures of a species have every atom in the same position and differ only in the positions of electrons (double bonds, lone pairs and the charges that go with them). Moving an atom gives a different species, an isomer, not a resonance structure.
items.misconception: Resonance structures can differ in the positions of atoms, so moving an H atom to another atom gives another resonance structure.
items.why: Resonance structures and isomers are both drawn as alternative formulas for the same molecular formula, and students do not separate moving electrons from moving atoms; confusing resonance with isomerism is a commonly reported difficulty in chemistry-education research. Before accepting a resonance structure, check that every atom is still bonded to the same atoms; only double bonds, lone pairs and charges may change position.
items.specStatementText: Resonance structures occur when there is more than one possible position for a double bond in a molecule.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does silicon, which conducts electricity slightly, have a layered structure like graphite?
items.correct: No. Silicon has the diamond structure: each Si atom is covalently bonded to four others in a three-dimensional network, and all four of its valence electrons are used in localized bonds. It conducts only slightly because it is a semiconductor, not because it has graphite's delocalized electrons.
items.misconception: A covalent network that conducts electricity, even slightly, must have graphite's structure: layers of atoms each bonded to three others, with delocalized electrons.
items.why: Graphite is the only conducting covalent network studied in detail, so 'conducts electricity' becomes linked to 'layers like graphite'; silicon is in group 14 with carbon, which makes the analogy with graphite seem natural. Decide the structure from the bonding: each Si atom forms four covalent bonds, as C does in diamond, so it has no delocalized electron per atom. Its slight conductivity is a semiconductor property.
items.specStatementText: Carbon and silicon form covalent network structures.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the two regions of electron density in a π bond, above and below the bond axis, two separate bonds?
items.correct: No. One π bond is one shared pair whose electron density lies in two regions on opposite sides of the bond axis. A double bond is one σ bond and one π bond.
items.misconception: The two lobes of a π bond, above and below the bond axis, are two separate bonds.
items.why: Orbital diagrams draw a π bond as two shaded regions, and students who count each shaded region as a bond arrive at three bonds for a double bond. Count one π bond for each pair of laterally overlapping p orbitals; its two lobes are the two halves of a single bond.
items.specStatementText: Sigma bonds σ form by the head-on combination of atomic orbitals where the electron density is concentrated along the bond axis. Pi bonds π form by the lateral combination of p-orbitals where the electron density is concentrated on opposite sides of the bond axis.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is an O=O bond the same strength as an O–O bond, because both are between two oxygen atoms?
items.correct: No. Bond enthalpy rises with the number of shared pairs: O–O is about 144 kJ mol⁻¹ and O=O 498 kJ mol⁻¹. The atoms bonded and the number of shared pairs both matter.
items.misconception: A bond between the same two elements has the same length and strength whatever the number of shared pairs.
items.why: Bond enthalpy tables are looked up by the pair of atoms, and students often use a single 'O–O' or 'C–C' value without checking whether the bond is single, double or triple. Identify the bond order first: single, double and triple bonds between the same two atoms have different lengths and different strengths.
items.specStatementText: Single, double and triple bonds involve one, two and three shared pairs of electrons respectively.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the resonance structures of a species isomers of it?
items.correct: No. Isomers are different species whose atoms are joined differently. Resonance structures of one species have every atom in the same place and differ only in where the electrons (double bonds, lone pairs, charges) are drawn; together they describe one real structure.
items.misconception: Resonance structures are isomers: different species with the same formula but different bonding.
items.why: Resonance structures and isomers are both drawn as alternative formulas for one molecular formula, and students do not separate moving electrons from moving atoms; confusing resonance with isomerism is widely reported in chemistry-education research. Check the atoms: if every atom is bonded to the same atoms in both drawings, they are resonance structures of one species, not isomers.
items.specStatementText: Resonance structures occur when there is more than one possible position for a double bond in a molecule.
